title: The Gate in the Park
markdown:
Elara traced a faint etching in her worn copy of Local Legends of Little Puddleton. She preferred dusty books to noisy games; her mind was a meticulous catalogue of dates and deeds. Beside her, cousin Jasper—who hailed from the decidedly less dusty year of 1888—was attempting to tie a knot in a long blade of grass. His brow furrowed. He had a perpetually surprised look, as if the modern world were a constant delightful puzzle he had not quite packed for.

“Most peculiar,” Elara murmured, not to Jasper, to the air, a low hum of curiosity.

Jasper, who usually answered with a hearty Great Scott or a bewildered blink, looked up from the grass. “What is? This blade? Unruly, I grant you. Almost as unruly as Mrs. Higgins’s prize petunias. Terrible temper, that woman.”

“No, Jasper. That.” She pointed, gaze fixed.

Where there had been a solid ancient oak moments before—bark like a dragon’s scales, branches reaching—there now stood a wrought-iron churchyard gate. Not any gate: impossibly ornate, verdigris-kissed, curves like ferns, spikes like tiny sleeping swords. It looked as though it had been guarding centuries of secrets and whispering them to the wind. The problem, the heart of the puzzle, was that there was no church to guard, no graveyard to enter, and certainly no gate in this well-trodden part of the park.

“Well, I’ll be jiggered!” Jasper dropped the grass as if it had become a worm. “Wasn’t there when I was admiring that remarkably robust pigeon. Exceptionally determined waddle.”

Elara’s neat mind felt like a teacup brimming. A tingle of knowing buzzed behind her eyes. This was not history going terribly wrong, like a misplaced comma in a treaty. This was history tripping over its own feet, a small embarrassing wobble in the tapestry. And wobbles, however small, needed fixing before they unravelled anything important.

She took a tentative step toward the shimmering iron. A small metallic object zipped out of thin air with a sound like a tiny startled bumblebee, hovered with an almost apologetic whir, and deposited a rather flustered tweed-clad individual onto the soft grass. The contraption then vanished as if embarrassed.

The man looked as though he had been surprised by his own socks and was still smoothing his rumpled waistcoat. He blinked owlishly through spectacles that were perpetually sliding. Wild grey hair defied gravity, a dandelion clock in a strong breeze.

“Fizzwick!” he announced, then blinked, remembering manners. “Forgive me. Designation Fizzwick. Temporal Assistance Operative, at your service. Albeit slightly delayed. Time is, as you may or may not know, rather bendy.” He fumbled a complicated device that emitted a faint peculiar scent of lavender and burnt toast.

Jasper’s eyes went wide. “Temporal Assistance Operative? A time policeman? Special hat?”

Fizzwick beamed a little too brightly. “Precisely! Well, not precisely. More a fixer of temporal foibles. And you two, I presume, are the designated historical custodians of this juncture? The ones who noticed the anomaly?”

Elara, who preferred solving problems without grand speeches, nodded slowly, gaze never leaving the gate. “We noticed. It’s misplaced. It simply should not be here.”

“Misplaced!” Fizzwick clapped; a puff of lavender escaped. “Classic nexus bleed. A small tear in causality. Echoes bleeding through. Nothing to worry about, really. Tiny bit of history getting jumbled. Jumbled history, as we all know, is bothersome to sort.” Spectacles slid. “The mission, should you choose to accept it, is to identify the source and patch it before undue historical embarrassment. A historical oopsie, if you will.”

Jasper, never shy of a challenge, puffed his chest until waistcoat buttons strained. “Jumbled history is my speciality. I once spilled an entire inkwell on Father’s most important ledger. Quite jumbled, that.”

Fizzwick consulted the whirring device. “Source appears Victoriana-adjacent… temporal strata. We must retrieve a misplaced teacup. Imperative! The very stability of the timeline might hinge upon it.”

Jasper’s eyes widened further. “Victoriana-adjacent sounds dreadfully like my drawing-room. I distinctly recall leaving my favourite cup—the one with the tiny painted robins—right by the fireplace.”

And so, with Fizzwick’s woefully inaccurate directions and Jasper’s escalating bewilderment, the quest began. The park, usually green, benches, cheerful dog-walkers, began to shimmer and shift. Air grew heavy, thick with old paper and damp wool. The clatter of unseen carriage wheels. A chill like forgotten secrets. A horse-drawn rattle passed where a modern bicycle should have been; the rider tipped an imaginary hat. Sparrows gave way to the faint melancholic call of gulls, though they were miles from the coast.

“Most irregular,” Jasper muttered, clutching his waistcoat as if to keep from floating. “The very air is whispering secrets. And not polite ones.”

Fizzwick wrestled a chronometer spinning like a child’s top wound too tight. “Odd. Flux is frisky. Terribly frisky. Scanner identifying a particularly significant anomaly… a squirrel? Plump specimen. Hardly a temporal threat.”

Elara ignored the squirrel. Her historian’s eye caught a path ahead that had not been there: a cliff path braided with sea-mist, curling with a life of its own, though the sun shone and the sea was miles off. The mist clung, cool and damp, rain on old stone, the faint sweet decay of leaves long gone to dust.

They found themselves in a place that was and was not the old cemetery. Tombstones at odd angles, some too new, inscriptions jarringly modern. One ancient moss-covered stone bore Agnes Buttercup, a name Elara vaguely recalled from a parish register. A lone gnarled yew, branches like skeletal fingers, stood sentinel near a mausoleum she swore she had never seen, granite weathered as if it had observed centuries.

“Temporal discombobulator registering strong emotional resonance,” Fizzwick announced, tapping until another pair of spectacles dislodged. “This way!” Great deal of arm-waving toward the yew. “Powerful echo of longing. And perhaps misplaced gardening tools?”

Elara, gaze on the mausoleum, noticed a faint inscription half-hidden by ivy: longing, a lost keepsake, a wish for return. Not a historical footnote. A memory. A heartfelt desire made masonry. This gate was not a tear in time so much as a doorway conjured by a man who could not let go.

“Reverend Silas Blackwood,” she breathed, the name clicking like a lost puzzle piece. A footnote from an obscure local-history pamphlet: a vicar vanished under peculiar circumstances in the early 1900s. Not a soul knew where he had gone.

Fizzwick’s device emitted alarming beeps, lights like a tiny panicked disco. “Warning! Temporal integrity degrading! Seal the nexus immediately or risk moderate inconvenience to the local populace! Never a good thing!”

Jasper, stating the obvious with gusto, asked, “What sort of inconvenience? Will the teacups start singing opera?”

“Perhaps,” Fizzwick squeaked, hair standing in a halo of static, “a sudden proliferation of enthusiastic Victorian milliners demanding silk ribbons? Or a plague of highly opinionated dodos?”

Elara stayed with the inscription. She imagined the Reverend aching for a moment of simple joy. “The keepsake,” she said softly, fingers tracing worn words, then the tarnished silver locket she spotted in the yew’s serpent roots. “The anchor of his longing.”

With a heave and a grunt, Jasper—surprising strength for so much enthusiasm—helped her dislodge a loose moss-covered stone. Beneath, in dark damp earth, the locket. When Elara picked it up, a wave of quiet sadness washed through her, a ghost of forgotten love that was not entirely hers. Peace, she realized. Not stopping history. Letting it rest.

Fizzwick, in a flurry, mashed buttons with more enthusiasm than accuracy. “Initiating temporal containment! Brace for historical confetti! Crucial to aesthetic reintegration!”

A loud POP. Bright shimmering paper rained, swirling in the misty air. Jasper, startled and amused, caught a glimpse of a prehistoric butterfly, iridescent, before it vanished too.

“Historical punctuation,” Fizzwick declared, wiping blue confetti from his nose into burnt-toast residue. “My own invention. Helps the timeline absorb more pleasingly.”

Elara ignored the festive chaos and the lavender. Eyes closed, locket warm. She imagined Silas Blackwood a little lonely, finally quieter. She placed the silver back in its earthy hollow beneath the stone, a gesture of respect, not a speech.

The impossible gate shimmered, verdigris brighter for a breath, then began to fade like a dream at dawn. Mist thinned. Old parchment and damp earth receded. Fresh-cut grass returned, distant traffic, children’s laughter.

Fizzwick, confetti in his wild hair like festive snow, gave a final enthusiastic wave, spectacles crooked. “All in a day’s work! History is best enjoyed tidy! Watch for rogue squirrels!” Another puff of lavender and toast, and he vanished, leaving a slightly singed patch and a linger of ozone.

Jasper looked around. The park ordinary. The oak stoic where the gate had been. “More exciting than my history lessons. Though I still maintain the pigeon was unusually robust. Gravitas, if you ask me.”

Elara smiled, quiet, as far as her eyes. The gate was gone. A man’s gentle longing had been acknowledged without a lecture. Jasper hummed a jaunty gaslight tune from his own time and walked beside her along a path that was, for the moment, exactly where a path ought to be, oak included, pigeon optional.
characters: Elara (thoughtful child historian), Jasper (a cousin from the wrong century)
audience: children aged 11-12, fantastic mystery adventure for older children
